2. The *poṣadha* of two or three people is called the *bahupoṣadha*.
3. The *poṣadha* of two people is called the *yugapoṣadha*.
4. The *poṣadha* of one person is called the *ekapoṣadha*.
The verse says:
"The wise person can understand the five kinds of self-indulgence.
The commentary says:
There are five types of *pravāraṇā-karman*:
first, when five groups perform the initial *pravāraṇā*, it is called the *saṃgha-pravāraṇā*.
Second, when four persons perform the *pravāraṇā*, it is called the *bahujana-pravāraṇā*.
3. Three people performing the *pravāraṇā* together is called "mutual *pravāraṇā*" (*dvaya-pravāraṇā*).
4. Two people performing the *pravāraṇā* [together].
5. One person performing the *pravāraṇā* alone; these are all called "individual *pravāraṇā*" (*eka-pravāraṇā*).
The verse says:
"The discernment of the requisites for the life of a śramaṇa is transmitted.
The commentary says:
The requisites of a śramaṇa refer to the alms bowl, the three robes, ghee and so forth, and the staff and pouch.
Regarding these, as for the alms bowl—whether it is present before one or not—it is sufficient that another person knows of its transmission for the procedure to be accomplished.

Regarding robes, if they are present before one, the transmission is accomplished through three successive handings over; or, if one causes another to know [the transmission], the transmission is likewise accomplished.
If they are not present before one, it is sufficient merely to cause another to know [the transmission] for the transmission to be accomplished.
Regarding items such as ghee and staff-cases, it is sufficient that another person knows they have been transmitted; there is no separate act of transmission.
The verse says:
"And understanding the five kinds of purity for śramaṇas."
The commentary states: There are five kinds of purity for śramaṇas:
first, injury by contact with fire; second, injury by weapons such as knives; third, self-inflicted injury; fourth, injury by birds and the like; and fifth, injury by claws and the like.
Among these, the first two are pure together with the kernels; the remaining three may only consume the skin and flesh, but not the kernels.
The verse says:
"The two persons—self and other—and that which is neither, can understand the purity of the śramaṇa's actions."
The commentary states:
There are four kinds of living beings produced from the aggregation of the four great elements:
first, those born from seeds; [and so forth].
2. Birth from roots;
3. Birth by segmentation;
4. Birth from the vapors of the four great elements.
That purity is of four kinds:

first, that produced by one's own preparatory effort; second, that produced by the preparatory effort of another; third, that produced by the preparatory efforts of both oneself and another; and fourth, that produced by neither one's own nor another's preparatory effort.
These four kinds of purification are not established with respect to a single object alone; if even one within a collection is purified, the remainder are all purified as well.
If a person can understand these meanings, they will be clear regarding the Vinaya.
The verse says:
The definitive meaning reveals the qualities of clarity, namely the fifty-five qualities of a venerable teacher.
Such a person is perfect and praised by the Buddhas, being endowed with the qualities of a master of the Vinaya.
The commentary states:
Regarding the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the person upon whom he relies, there are five sets of five virtues.
If one possesses even one of these five virtues, such a person is qualified to act as a preceptor and a teacher of reliance (*niśraya-ācārya*).
The five kinds of fifty [aspects] are:
first, understanding the characteristics of offenses;
second, understanding the characteristics of the causal origination of offenses.
Third, understanding the characteristics of what is not an offense;
fourth, understanding the methods for emerging from an offense;
fifth, having ten years of seniority.
This is the first set of five:
first, possessing ethical discipline;
second, being learned.
Third, great wisdom;
fourth, the ability to attend to the sick;
fifth, ten years of seniority—this is the second set of five.
First, possessing ethical discipline;
second, being well-learned;
third, possessing great wisdom.
Fourth, the capacity to discern and cause one to be free from all views regarding their essence and function;
fifth, ten years of ordination.
These constitute the third set of five.
First, possessing ethical discipline;
second, being learned;
third, possessing great wisdom.
Fourth, one who is capable of leading others out of regions where there are difficulties;
fifth, one with ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*).
These are the fourth and fifth [qualifications].
First, possessing the precepts;
second, being able to attend to the sick;
third, being able to cause them to be free from remorse and regret.
Fourth, the capacity to discern and thereby cause one to be free from all views, both in essence and function;
fifth, ten years of seniority.
This is the fifth pentad.
Precepts, illness, remorse, various views, and ten years of seniority—this is the sixth pentad.
Precepts, illness, remorse, extensive learning, and ten years of seniority—this is the seventh pentad.
Precepts, illness, remorse, great wisdom, and ten years of seniority—this is the eighth set of five.
Precepts, illness, various views, extensive learning, and ten years of seniority—this is the ninth set of five.
Precepts, illness, various views, great wisdom, and ten years of seniority—this is the fifteenth.
These combined constitute the first set of fifty.
Precepts, illness, difficult regions, extensive learning, and ten years of seniority—these are the first five.
Virtue, freedom from illness, extensive learning, great wisdom, and ten years of seniority—this is the second set of five.
Perfection in virtue, being endowed with right conduct, being endowed with right view, being able to attend to the sick, and ten years of seniority—this is the third set of five.
The fifth pentad consists of: precepts, being free from illness, extensive learning, the ability to eliminate arisen or unarisen remorse and regret, and ten years of seniority.
The sixth pentad consists of: precepts, right conduct, right view, freedom from all [wrong] views, and ten years of seniority.
Precepts, right conduct, right view, skillful means, and ten years of seniority—this is the sixth pentad.
Precepts, right conduct, right view, extensive learning, and ten years of seniority—this is the seventh pentad.
Virtue, right conduct, right view, great wisdom, and ten years of standing—this is the eighth pentad.
Virtue, right conduct, right view, being able to instruct disciples in the training of the higher morality, and ten years of standing—this is the ninth pentad.
Virtue, right conduct, right view, being able to instruct disciples in the training that relies on the mind, and having ten years of seniority—this is the fifteenth [requirement].
This combined constitutes the second set of fifty.
There are also five [qualities] regarding the ability to teach disciples in the training of wisdom; this is the first set of five.
Among these three [trainings], being able to cause oneself to study diligently for ten years of seniority constitutes the third set of five.
To be able to instruct disciples in the training regarding the basis and the right practice for ten years—this is the fifth set of five.
To be able to instruct disciples in the training regarding the basis and the holy life for ten years.
This is the sixth set of five.
Being able to instruct disciples in the training based on the Prātimokṣa for ten years is the seventh set of five.
Being able to diligently train oneself in three areas for ten years constitutes the third set of five.
This combination constitutes the third set of fifty.
Precepts, right conduct, right view, and the ability to instruct disciples regarding the training rules (*śaikṣa-śīla*) for ten years constitute the first set of five.

Regarding those based on trainee concentration (*śaikṣa-samādhi*), there are also five; regarding those based on trainee wisdom (*śaikṣa-prajñā*), there are also five; regarding those based on trainee liberation (*śaikṣa-vimukti*), there are also five; regarding those based on trainee knowledge and vision of liberation (*śaikṣa-vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), there are also five; and among these five, for those who can diligently train themselves and have ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*), there are likewise five sets of five.
Combining [the categories] of self and others, this constitutes the fourth set of fifty.

Precepts, right conduct, and right view—being able to instruct disciples regarding the training rules of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*) and having ten years of seniority—constitute the first set of five.

Regarding those based on the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are five; regarding those based on the wisdom of one beyond training, there are five; regarding those based on the liberation of one beyond training, there are five; and regarding those based on the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training, there are five. Within these five categories, there are five for each instance of being able to diligently train oneself and having ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). When combined according to both self and others, this constitutes the fifth set of fifty.
These five sets of fifty virtues can clearly manifest a person.
If a person can discern such meanings, that person studies what the Buddha has taught and is endowed with the qualities corresponding to those of a Vinaya Master.
The verse says:
One who has a definitive understanding of these meanings through the practice of reciting the texts and serving the teacher is clear regarding the Vinaya;
the Buddha said that such a person does not rely on others.
The commentary states:

In such places as previously described, if a person has thoroughly mastered the recitation of the textual passages, has completed the discernment of their meaning, and has finished practicing the application of the matter, that person is then proficient in the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Buddha said that because this person is free from ignorance and does not give rise to doubt, they possess mastery over the three meanings and do not look to the countenances of others.
The root verse says:

"That which is revealed by the texts of Vinaya and Abhidharma, for those who correspond with the precepts and their protection, and who cultivate the three trainings praised by all Buddhas—without looking to the faces of others, I shall now speak."

This root verse constitutes the Dharma Master’s solemn vow, stating: "I shall explain this *Viniścaya* (Clarification), by means of which these and other such causes and conditions will reveal the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This vow has now been fulfilled; the *Viniścayasamgrahaṇī-śāstra* in twenty-two [sections] is hereby completed.

This treatise was composed by the Dharma Master Buddhatrāta, a non-returner (anāgāmin), who, out of compassion for those intimidated by voluminous texts, has here concisely summarized the meaning of the Vinaya.

The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, one fascicle. On the twentieth day of the first month in the second year of the Guangda era of the Chen dynasty, the cyclical year being Wuzi, the Vinaya Master Fatai of Dinglin Monastery in the capital requested the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇarata to translate this treatise within Nanhai Commandery in Guangzhou.
Hui Kai of Ayuwang Monastery in the capital respectfully served as the scribe.
The translation of the root treatise consists of one fascicle, while the annotated commentary and explanations comprise five fascicles.

The treatise contains twenty-two verses that summarize the long prose sections on the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*. In some instances, the verses follow the meaning of the prose, while in others, they are explained by breaking down the phrasing; thus, the various lines do not always correspond directly to one another.
I now respectfully excerpt twenty-two verses and place them at the end of this volume, so that those who read the text may see its beginning and conclusion.
The Abhidharma and Vinaya texts reveal the person who is in accord with the precepts and their protection;
one who is praised by all Buddhas for practicing the three trainings—without looking to the faces of others, I shall now speak of them.
The eight precepts and protections are ninety-six; Their distinct meanings are analyzed in accordance with reality.
Twice twenty-one thousand rivers of merit flow forth, Washing away defilements with the waters of wholesome Dharma.
He understands the five characteristics and nine rules of discipline of the precepts; he understands the five classes of offenses and eight origins;
he understands the seven groups of offenses and the five forms of confession; and he understands the four kinds of loss and the four kinds of attainment.
He is able to skillfully discern the three corners of transgression; understanding the reality of conceptualization, he establishes the training rules.
Regarding the precepts established by nature and those established by convention, he can analyze and explain them according to principle.
Discerning the deeds performed by the two classes [of beings], Understanding the categories of what constitutes a schism and what does not, as well as the timing;
Understanding the minor and secondary precepts, as well as those that are not minor; Discerning the proper methods for entering households.
He was well-versed in the three ways of rising from offenses and the three methods for manifesting and confessing them;
he established the origins of the precepts and distinguished their reductions and extensions, skillfully analyzing these matters extensively according to the texts.
The offenses and non-offenses as recorded by the Buddha, And as adjudicated in the Vinaya and Abhidharma—
Thoroughly understanding each offense and non-offense, As well as the five methods for the arising of higher offenses.
Skilled in understanding the four kinds of relinquishment, Skilled in understanding the three robes and the six objects of compassion,
Discerning the four types of offenses within the Vinaya, And regarding the six precepts, understanding the four relatives who should be approached.
One attains perfect qualities through the seven bases of dependence; discerns the characteristics of the two types of perfect qualities;
skillfully understands the five kinds of unreal speech; and knows the categories for cultivating the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
One is able to understand the four conditions for sustaining life, one is able to accomplish the five types of portions for receiving food,
and regarding the ten kinds of *kṛtānna* (leftover food) procedures, one is able to understand and practice each of those methods in their respective regions.
One is able to understand the seven causes for the loss of alms-food, as well as the three types of contact that cause food not yet received to be lost;
one discerns the five ways in which food fails to be properly prepared, as well as the four ways of losing it through contact, of which there are five types.
If difficulties arise during the seven days, one may travel as desired;

One should skillfully understand the three types and nine categories, Understand the five factors that enable the completion of the summer retreat, And understand the eight kinds of difficulties regarding the summer retreat.
Having discerned the merits and faults of the five types of formal procedures, such as the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*,
and having well understood the Buddha’s intent in establishing the precepts within the four categories of prohibited training rules.
Skillfully understanding the three measurements of bowls and robes, their successive transmission, their formal acceptance, and their reliance on vows;
one must determine the measurements of bowls and robes in two locations, according to the time, the offense, the interval, and the direction.
In these instances, the means, the owner, and the property can bring about a *niḥsargika* offense;
all such matters, according to their sequence, enable one to understand the thirty rules of training.
He is well able to discern the eight rules of respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*), understands the methods and sequence of the characteristics of the correct teaching,
and within the four stages beginning with the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), he understands the methods and the five bases of formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
Skillfully understanding the five types of attainment, And understanding the transgressions of the Vinaya through five gateways—
Regarding the offenses arising from entry and boundaries, One understands them as they are adjudicated in the world.
Understanding the eight ways of lifting the kaṭhina, as well as the five merits of the kaṭhina;
skillfully understanding that the two types of guardians do not obtain the precepts; the twenty persons and the ten bases for confession.
Skillfully understanding the two types of restraint to prevent unwholesome contact, Comprehending the four *karmas* as well as reliance on tranquility,
Able to distinguish the four types of *poṣadha* rites, The wise person can thoroughly understand the five types of *pravāraṇā*.
Having thoroughly understood the transmission of the requisites for a śramaṇa, And having mastered the five kinds of purity for a śramaṇa—
Whether pertaining to oneself, another, both, or neither— One is able to understand the purity of the śramaṇa's activities.
The definitive meaning can reveal the quality of clarity, namely the qualities of the fifty-five venerable masters;
this person is praised by the Perfect Buddha as being endowed with the qualities of a master of the Vinaya.
One who has reached a definitive understanding of these meanings through the practice of reciting the texts and serving the teacher is clearly proficient in the Vinaya;
the Buddha said that such a person does not rely on others.
